---
title: "A longer read"
---

This page is deliberately long. It exists to be scrolled, so the reading-progress bar at the
top fills as you move down, the "minutes left" estimate counts toward zero, and your position
is remembered: close the tab partway through and a *Resume reading* pill brings you back to
the exact block you left, anchored to that block's content hash rather than a raw scroll
offset, so it survives a re-render or a change of window size.

## On length

A long document is not a failure of editing; sometimes the subject is large. What a long
document owes its reader is orientation. A printed book gives it for free: the heft in your
left hand versus your right tells you, without a word, how far you have come and how far is
left. A web page gives you nothing. The scrollbar is a poor substitute, thin and easy to
ignore, and it measures pixels, not ideas. A reader deep in a forty-minute chapter, with no
sense of the end, reads differently than one who can see the shore.

## On memory

The second thing a long read owes its reader is memory. Reading is rarely done in one sitting.
You stop to think, to eat, to sleep, and you come back. A tool that forgets where you were
punishes the very act of returning, which is the act most worth encouraging. The browser's
native scroll restoration is unreliable and coarse; it remembers a pixel offset that means
nothing after the layout reflows on a different screen. Anchoring to a block's identity is
exact, and it is the kind of thing qmd-fast can do that a plain web page cannot, because every
block already carries a stable, content-derived id.

## On estimates

People ask "how long will this take?" before they ask "is this any good?". An honest estimate,
even a rough one, is a kindness: it lets the reader choose the right moment. Reading speed
varies, so the number is approximate by nature, and that is fine. Counting the prose and
ignoring the code and the equations gives a figure close enough to be useful and never
pretends to a precision it does not have.

## On restraint

The danger with reading aids is that they crowd the page. A progress bar that pulses, a
counter that jumps, a pill that nags: each one steals attention from the words, which is the
opposite of the point. The right amount of chrome is the least amount that still answers the
reader's two quiet questions, *where am I* and *can I come back*, and then gets out of the
way. A thin bar, a small number, a pill that appears once and then dismisses itself.

## A middle section

Here is more prose so the page is genuinely long. The measure of a reading surface is not how
much it can show but how little it asks. Every control is a small tax on attention. The ones
worth keeping are the ones a reader would miss if they were gone, and would not think about
while they were there. Orientation and memory pass that test. They are invisible until needed
and obvious the moment they are.

## Another section

The same logic that makes the live editor fast, a stable block model with content-hash ids,
is what makes the reader's position durable. The architecture that was built for the author
pays the reader too. That is the recurring shape of qmd-fast's best features: one structural
idea, the identified block, cashed in two directions at once.

## On finishing

A reader who reaches the end of a long piece has given you something scarce, their sustained
attention, and the least you can do is make the journey legible while it happens. By the time
these words are on screen the progress bar should be near full and the estimate near zero. The
end of a document is a small event worth marking quietly, not with confetti, just with the
honest absence of any more bar to fill.

## The end

There is nothing after this heading except the satisfaction of having arrived. If your
position was saved on the way down, reloading this page should offer to bring you back to
wherever you were, not here.
